overview: Carcharodontosaurus saharicus was a massive carcharodontosaurid theropod from the Cenomanian of North Africa (~100–94 Ma), rivalling Tyrannosaurus in length and sharing its continent with Spinosaurus in a vast river-delta ecosystem. Its name — "shark-toothed lizard" — refers to its large, flattened, serrated teeth convergent with those of great white sharks.

The original specimens, described by Stromer in 1931, were destroyed in the 1944 Allied bombing of Munich. New material described by Sereno and colleagues in 1996 from Morocco provided a far more complete picture of this giant predator and confirmed it as a carcharodontosaurid distinct from South American relatives.

fossilSites.name: Kem Kem Group
fossilSites.note: Cenomanian fluvial deposits yielding the best-known Carcharodontosaurus material alongside Spinosaurus, Deltadromeus and a diverse fish fauna.

fossilSites.name: Bahariya Formation
fossilSites.note: Type locality for the original Stromer specimens, destroyed in WWII; additional fragmentary material has since been recovered.

articles.title: Discovery and the WWII loss
articles.body: Ernst Stromer described Carcharodontosaurus saharicus in 1931 from Bahariya Formation material, alongside Spinosaurus aegyptiacus and the giant crocodilian Stomatosuchus. The Munich collection housing these unique specimens was destroyed in an Allied bombing raid on 24 April 1944. New material from the Kem Kem Group described by Sereno in 1996 not only confirmed Carcharodontosaurus but showed it to be larger than previously thought.

articles.title: Anatomy and size
articles.body: The skull reaches approximately 1.6 m in length, with large blade-like teeth bearing serrations on both edges. The overall body plan is typical for a large carcharodontosaurid: robust axial skeleton, powerful hindlimbs and relatively gracile forelimbs with three-fingered hands. Size estimates place large individuals at 12–13 m, making it one of the largest terrestrial predators from Africa.

articles.title: North African mega-predator ecosystem
articles.body: The Kem Kem deposits record a dramatic ecosystem where multiple giant predators coexisted — Carcharodontosaurus, Spinosaurus, Deltadromeus and large crocodilians in a river-delta environment rich in fish. How these apex predators partitioned resources is debated; Spinosaurus' aquatic specialisation likely segregated it from the terrestrially hunting Carcharodontosaurus, reducing direct competition.

fossilRecord.formations: Bahariya Formation, Egypt; Kem Kem Group, Morocco
fossilRecord.material: Skull fragments, teeth and partial skeletal material from North African Cretaceous deposits.
fossilRecord.paleo: Cretaceous North African river and coastal systems with giant theropods, sauropods and abundant fish.
fossilRecord.evidence: Large blade-like serrated teeth and skull material define its carcharodontosaurid identity.

record.description: Carcharodontosaurus saharicus was a giant carcharodontosaurid from Cenomanian North Africa. The name originated with now-lost Algerian teeth and is stabilised by a large partial Moroccan neotype skull; the destroyed Egyptian skeleton long used to reconstruct it was separated in 2025 as Tameryraptor markgrafi.
facts: The Moroccan neotype SGM-Din 1 preserves a large but incomplete skull, not a full skeleton.
Postcranial and crest details from the Bahariya specimen named Tameryraptor must no longer be presented as C. saharicus anatomy.

presentation.heroLead: A giant shark-toothed predator of Cretaceous North Africa, whose name now rests on a single large partial skull from Morocco rather than on the lost Egyptian skeleton once used to reconstruct it.

heroMedia.title: Life restoration of Carcharodontosaurus saharicus

heroMedia.caption: Life restoration by Fred Wierum. The skull follows the Moroccan neotype; the body is modelled on the related Giganotosaurus because secure postcranial bones of Carcharodontosaurus are scarce. Colour and skin are interpretive.

animalParagraphs: Carcharodontosaurus was a very large two-legged predator of the carcharodontosaurid family, named for its blade-like, serrated teeth that reminded early describers of those of the great white shark. The Moroccan neotype skull is about 1.6 metres long, which places the animal among the largest theropods known. Whole-body estimates of twelve to thirteen metres and several tonnes are extrapolations from that skull using the proportions of relatives such as Giganotosaurus.

The skull is long and relatively narrow, with a large opening in front of the eye, thin, ornamented nasal and lacrimal bones and a lightly built braincase. CT study of the neotype braincase shows a small, elongate brain with large olfactory bulbs and a relatively small optic region, a pattern shared with other allosauroids.

It lived on the river deltas and floodplains of the Kem Kem region alongside Spinosaurus, the abelisaurids and Deltadromeus. Much of the body plan, limb proportions and any behaviour attributed to it in popular accounts come from other carcharodontosaurids, because the securely referred fossils of Carcharodontosaurus itself are almost entirely cranial.
animalHighlights: Blade-like teeth with wrinkled enamel bands across the crown, a feature shared by the family that bears its name.
A large, lightly built skull with a long snout, thin skull roof bones and a small braincase, all directly seen in the neotype.
A body reconstructed from relatives: postcranial anatomy is not securely known for the genus after the 2025 removal of the Egyptian specimen.

lifeCards.label: Feeding
lifeCards.level: Supported by teeth and skull anatomy
lifeCards.reason: Serrated, laterally compressed teeth and a slicing skull architecture indicate a predator of large animals. Prey is inferred from the Kem Kem fauna; no gut contents or bite-marked bones are securely attributed.

lifeCards.label: Movement
lifeCards.reason: No secure hindlimb of C. saharicus is known. Bipedal posture follows every other large theropod and the closely related Giganotosaurus.

lifeCards.label: Known size
lifeCards.reason: The neotype skull is measurable; body length of twelve to thirteen metres and mass of six tonnes or more depend on scaling from relatives.

lifeCards.label: Appearance
lifeCards.reason: Skull shape is known from the neotype. Body proportions, skin texture and colour are borrowed from better-known carcharodontosaurids.

locality.name: Kem Kem beds
locality.note: Kem Kem Group, Cenomanian. The original type teeth came from the Continental Intercalaire near Timimoun, Algeria, and are lost; the neotype skull was collected in Morocco in 1995.

presentation.classificationSummary: Carcharodontosaurus is the name-bearing genus of Carcharodontosauridae, a family of large allosauroid theropods that also includes Giganotosaurus, Mapusaurus and Acrocanthosaurus. Its closest relatives are the South American giganotosaurines; the second species, C. iguidensis from Niger, may not belong in the genus.

related.reason: A closely related South American carcharodontosaurid known from a much more complete skeleton, on which body reconstructions of Carcharodontosaurus depend.
An earlier North American carcharodontosaurian with a well-preserved skull and skeleton for comparison.
The other giant predator of the Kem Kem beds, found in the same Cenomanian rocks.

questions.title: How much of the classic skeleton was really Carcharodontosaurus?
questions.copy: The Egyptian skull and partial skeleton described by Stromer in 1931 were destroyed in 1944. Their re-evaluation from Stromer's records led to their separation as Tameryraptor in 2025, so older reconstructions of the body may not represent the Moroccan animal.

questions.title: How big was it?
questions.copy: Only the skull is securely measurable. Length and mass estimates rely on scaling from Giganotosaurus and other relatives, so published figures vary considerably.

questions.title: Is C. iguidensis a Carcharodontosaurus?
questions.copy: The Niger species was named in 2007 on a partial skull and braincase. Later analyses have questioned whether it belongs in the same genus, and its status remains under review.

review.ageReviewNote: Secure C. saharicus evidence is Cenomanian, chiefly the historical Algerian type record and the Kem Kem Group neotype of Morocco.

evidence.material: Now-lost type teeth documented historically, one large partial neotype skull and limited comparable cranial remains; no secure complete skeleton.
evidence.confidenceLimit: Skull size is clear, but total length and mass are extrapolated because secure postcrania are scarce.
uncertainties: C. iguidensis may not remain in the same genus.
Many isolated North African teeth and bones are not diagnostic.
The 2025 Tameryraptor revision is recent and should be monitored.

specimens.note: Large partial skull with braincase from the Kem Kem beds of Morocco, designated neotype by Sereno et al. in 1996.

specimens.name: Original type teeth
specimens.institution: Formerly Muséum d'Histoire naturelle, Lyon collections
specimens.note: Teeth from the Continental Intercalaire near Timimoun, Algeria, named Megalosaurus saharicus by Depéret and Savornin; now lost.

specimens.name: Bahariya specimen (now Tameryraptor)
specimens.note: Partial skull and skeleton described by Stromer in 1931, destroyed in 1944 and renamed Tameryraptor markgrafi in 2025.

panel.headline: Lost type teeth, a destroyed skeleton, and one large partial skull that now carries the name.
panel.standfirst: Carcharodontosaurus saharicus has an unusually tangled evidence base. The original Algerian teeth are lost, the Egyptian skeleton described in 1931 was destroyed in the Second World War and has since been reassigned to Tameryraptor, and the name is stabilised by a partial Moroccan skull designated as neotype in 1996.

coverage.label: Moderate
coverage.basis: A large partial skull with braincase is securely known. Secure postcranial material is very limited, and many isolated North African teeth and bones cannot be confidently referred.

knownRemains.title: What is actually preserved?
knownRemains.summary: The neotype SGM-Din 1 preserves much of the skull, including the maxilla, nasal, lacrimal, postorbital, jugal, part of the skull roof and a braincase, with teeth. Isolated teeth and a few bones from the Kem Kem beds and elsewhere have been referred to the species with varying confidence.
knownRemains.note: Postcranial features once attributed to Carcharodontosaurus came from the destroyed Bahariya specimen. After its separation as Tameryraptor markgrafi in 2025, those details should no longer be presented as C. saharicus anatomy.

media.title: Neotype skull with known bones in white
media.alt: Line diagram of the Carcharodontosaurus saharicus neotype skull in side view with preserved bones shown in white and reconstructed areas in grey
media.caption: A diagram of the neotype skull: white areas are preserved bone, grey areas are restored from relatives such as Acrocanthosaurus and Meraxes. The specimen appears in some sources under a University of Chicago catalogue number.

materialGroups.label: Skull and jaws
materialGroups.value: A large partial skull with braincase and teeth (the neotype), plus isolated teeth and a fragmentary dentary referred to the species.

materialGroups.label: Vertebral column
materialGroups.value: No securely referred vertebral series. Isolated Kem Kem vertebrae have been assigned to the genus but cannot be tied to the neotype.

materialGroups.label: Girdles and limbs
materialGroups.value: No secure girdle or limb elements; the classic limb material belonged to the destroyed Egyptian specimen now named Tameryraptor.

materialGroups.label: Exceptional preservation
materialGroups.value: The neotype braincase has been CT-scanned to reconstruct the brain and inner ear. No skin, colour or gut contents are known.

specimenCards.title: SGM-Din 1 · neotype
specimenCards.description: A partial skull collected from the Kem Kem beds of Morocco in 1995 and designated neotype by Sereno and colleagues in 1996, because the original Algerian teeth named by Depéret and Savornin in the 1920s are lost and the Egyptian material described by Stromer was destroyed in 1944.

specimenCards.title: Bahariya skull and skeleton · destroyed
specimenCards.description: A partial skull, vertebrae, pelvis and hindlimb bones from Egypt described by Stromer in 1931 and lost in the bombing of Munich in 1944. Known only from Stromer's descriptions and photographs, they were named Tameryraptor markgrafi in 2025.

interpretation.label: Directly observed
interpretation.value: A partial skull and braincase from Morocco, isolated shark-like teeth, and historical records of destroyed Egyptian bones.

interpretation.label: Scientific interpretation
interpretation.value: A giant carcharodontosaurid apex predator of Cenomanian North Africa, comparable in size to Giganotosaurus and Tyrannosaurus.

interpretation.label: Still unknown
interpretation.value: Body proportions, total length and mass, limb anatomy, the status of C. iguidensis and which isolated North African bones belong to the genus.

panel.limitations: The coverage band describes the securely referred material of C. saharicus at genus level after the 2025 revision. It is an editorial evidence summary, not a published completeness percentage, and it excludes isolated teeth of uncertain identity.
